passage:
Back at the school hostel after the science trip, the Class 10 girls kept retelling the bus breakdown. "The driver shouted at the mechanic," Ishita said. "And smoke poured out of the engine," someone added. "We had to walk to the dhaba in the dark."
Aditi had been asleep for most of it, headphones on. But by the third night of retelling, she was adding, "I saw the smoke. It was grey and smelled like burnt rubber."
When the warden showed the trip photos, there was no smoke, and it was still light when they walked. Aditi looked at the screen, confused. "But I remember it," she whispered.
Ishita said, "Honestly, I think I added the smoke too."

qa.q: What was Aditi doing during most of the breakdown?
qa.a: Aditi had been asleep for most of it, headphones on.

qa.q: Why did Aditi whisper, "But I remember it"?
qa.a: Hearing the story three nights in a row made the smoke and the dark feel like her own memories, so the photos felt strange to her.

qa.q: What could the group do to keep shared stories more accurate?
qa.a: They could check photos early, as the warden did, and say "I didn't see that myself" when repeating someone else's detail.

qa.q: What does Ishita's admission suggest about the others' memories?
qa.a: If even Ishita added the smoke, the group's retelling changed everyone's version, not only Aditi's.

grounding: It shows a teenager who absorbs friends' retellings of a shared trip and comes to remember things she never saw.

passage:
Dear Varun,
Something weird happened with the football match story. You know how everyone keeps telling it at lunch: the referee's whistle breaking, you slipping in the mud, Coach laughing so hard he had to sit down?
Yesterday I told it to my cousin with all those bits, as if I'd seen them. Then my cousin said, "Weren't you in the washroom for the second half?" I was! I missed the whole thing. I have no idea whether the whistle broke or whether Coach sat down. I've heard it so many times that it feels like I watched it.
So I'm asking you: what actually happened? I'll trust your version over mine for now.
Pema

qa.q: Where was Pema during the second half?
qa.a: Pema was in the washroom for the second half.

qa.q: Why did Pema tell the story like an eyewitness?
qa.a: Hearing it again and again at lunch made the whistle and the mud feel like things Pema had watched, so it seemed like a real memory.

qa.q: What choice does Pema make at the end, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Pema asks Varun what actually happened and decides to trust that version for now, since Varun was really on the field.

qa.q: How might Varun feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Varun might laugh at being asked, but also value Pema's honesty and take care to separate what Varun truly saw from what others added.

grounding: It shows a teenager who realises that friends' repeated retellings of a match have become a personal memory of events never seen.

passage:
Okay, Parul, is this recording? Good. My strange memory is from the terrace, two winters ago. A group of us were lighting sparklers, and a spark landed on Neel's sleeve. Everyone tells it the same way: he yelled, jumped into a bucket of water, and the bucket tipped over.
I told that story for a year. I could see the bucket rolling. Then Neel himself told me, "There was no bucket. I just shook my arm and it went out." And I thought, no, I remember the bucket! But when I checked, I'd gone downstairs for matches right then.
The bucket came from Joel's version. It moved into my head and sat there like mine.
Now I say, "I heard that..." if I didn't see it. I'm Vasudha, by the way.

qa.q: Where had Vasudha gone at the moment the spark fell?
qa.a: Vasudha had gone downstairs for matches right then.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha feel sure about the rolling bucket?
qa.a: Vasudha had told the story for a year and could see the bucket, even though it came from Joel's version; repeating it made the detail feel owned.

qa.q: What habit did Vasudha adopt, and why does it help?
qa.a: Vasudha says "I heard that..." when not an eyewitness, which keeps borrowed details apart from real memories.

qa.q: How might Neel feel hearing the bucket story told for a year?
qa.a: Neel might be amused or a little annoyed, since the story made his moment more dramatic than it was and nobody asked him.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose memory of a shared incident took on a detail that only a friend had described.

passage: I'm Tanuja, Nikita's older sister. Nikita's class went to Bhimtal lake last month. Nikita was in the second boat with her friend Pooja; the drama happened in the first boat. I know because Nikita phoned me that night: "Didi, did you hear? A snake swam next to Juhi's boat and Mohan almost fell in!" Since then her friends have told the story at our house twice, louder each time, the snake getting longer. Yesterday Nikita told our cousins, "The snake swam right past me, and I grabbed Mohan's shirt so he wouldn't fall." She said it with total certainty, eyes wide. I reminded her she was in the second boat. She frowned. "No, I was there. I can see its head in the water." I don't think she's lying. I think she's heard it so often it's become hers.

qa.q: Which boat was Nikita in?
qa.a: The second boat, with her friend Pooja.

qa.q: How does Nikita feel about being in the snake story, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nikita feels completely sure and excited, telling it with wide eyes and frowning when reminded she was in the second boat, because her friends' retellings blended into her memory.

qa.q: How could Tanuja help Nikita without calling her a liar?
qa.a: Tanuja could explain that group stories often blend into our own memories, and suggest asking Pooja what the second boat actually saw.

qa.q: How might Mohan feel hearing Nikita say she grabbed his shirt?
qa.a: Mohan might be confused, since he remembers no one from the other boat grabbing him, and may wonder where the detail came from.

grounding: A sister watches a teenager come to remember a boat incident she only heard friends describe, as group retelling blends into her memory.

passage:
Wednesday: The fire alarm rang during chemistry lab. Rukmini, fifteen, was in the washroom down the corridor and came out to find everyone lined up on the field. Aparna whispered, "A test tube cracked on the burner. Smoke everywhere."
Thursday: At lunch the story grew. "It was a small explosion," someone said. "Glass flew," said another. "Sir's eyebrows got singed!" Everyone laughed. Rukmini laughed too, picturing it.
Monday: At dinner Rukmini told her mother, "I was right there when the test tube blew up. A bit of glass hit my sleeve." Her mother looked alarmed. Aparna, visiting, put down her spoon. "Rukku, you were in the washroom." Rukmini opened her mouth to argue, then stopped. She could see the glass. She just couldn't remember seeing it.

qa.q: Where was Rukmini when the fire alarm rang?
qa.a: In the washroom down the corridor.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini feel sure, at dinner, that she had seen the glass?
qa.a: She pictured it while laughing with her friends, and that imagined picture blended into her memory until it felt like her own.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do when Aparna corrected her, and why was that a good choice?
qa.a: She stopped instead of arguing, which let her notice that she could picture the scene but not actually remember seeing it.

qa.q: What is it like for Aparna to hear Rukmini retell a scene she missed?
qa.a: Aparna is startled enough to put down her spoon; she knows where Rukmini really was, so she has to speak up gently and correct a friend in front of her mother.

grounding: Over several days, a teenager who missed a lab incident absorbs her friends' retellings and comes to remember being there.

passage:
"And then Sir slipped on the rocks and fell right into the river!" Avni was laughing so hard that the words barely came out. "I'll never forget his face."
Trisha raised an eyebrow. "Avni, you weren't there."
"Of course I was."
"You were on the bus with a headache. Remember? You missed the whole river walk."
Avni stopped laughing. "But I can see it. His glasses flew off, he grabbed a branch..."
"Because Harman told that story about ten times on the way home. With actions."
"No, I..." Avni went quiet. The headache. The bus seat. The window. Those were memories too.
"So which one's real?" Avni asked slowly.
"The bus," Trisha said gently. "The river is Harman's."

qa.q: Where was Avni during the river walk?
qa.a: Avni was on the bus with a headache.

qa.q: Why could Avni 'see' the teacher falling so clearly?
qa.a: Avni felt certain and amused, because hearing Harman's story many times, with actions, had blended into Avni's own memory.

qa.q: What could help Avni sort shared stories from personal memories?
qa.a: Asking 'Was I actually there?' and checking with friends like Trisha before telling a story as one's own.

qa.q: How did Trisha handle Avni's mistaken memory?
qa.a: Trisha pointed it out gently and explained where the river story came from, without making fun of Avni.

grounding: Shows a teenager remembering a trip incident she only heard friends describe, as if she had seen it.

passage: For two years I told people I had seen smoke pouring out of the chemistry lab the day the fire alarm went off in Class 9. I'm Jahnavi, and I really believed it. I could picture grey smoke curling under the door. Then at our farewell, Lalit dug out the school newsletter from that week. It had been a surprise drill. No smoke, no fire, nothing in the lab. I argued at first. But then I remembered where I'd been: in the library, on the other side of the building. The smoke came from the story we all told afterwards in the canteen, again and again, each person adding a bit. Somewhere in there, Lalit's "I think I saw smoke" had become my memory. It's strange to lose something you were sure you saw.

qa.q: Where was Jahnavi when the alarm went off?
qa.a: In the library, on the other side of the building.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel on learning it was a drill?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt defensive at first, then strange and unsettled at losing something Jahnavi had been sure of seeing.

qa.q: What did Lalit's newsletter show, and what could Jahnavi learn from it?
qa.a: That it was a surprise drill with no smoke; group retellings can plant details, so records help check memories.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel about having started the smoke story?
qa.a: Lalit might feel amused and a bit sheepish that a passing 'I think I saw smoke' became everyone's memory.

grounding: Shows a teenager who remembered seeing smoke that came only from friends' repeated retellings.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, girls' block, 18 August.
On Sunday night, Sarita said she saw a white shape on the terrace. By Monday, six girls had seen it, and by Tuesday Tenzin was telling me in detail how the shape floated past her window and whispered her name. When I asked where she was at the time, she said she was in bed, asleep, until the others woke her. Her room faces the courtyard, not the terrace. I don't think she is lying; she was upset and sure. Group stories at night grow quickly, and she had heard this one told many times at dinner. I showed the girls the white bedsheet that had blown off the terrace line, and we talked about how shared stories can feel like our own memories. I've also arranged for the terrace to be locked at night.

qa.q: Which way does Tenzin's room face?
qa.a: Tenzin's room faces the courtyard, not the terrace.

qa.q: Why was Tenzin so sure the shape whispered her name?
qa.a: Tenzin felt frightened and certain, because hearing the story told many times at dinner had blended into her own memory of that night.

qa.q: What did the warden do, and why was it a good approach?
qa.a: The warden showed the girls the blown-off bedsheet and talked about how shared stories become memories, without calling Tenzin a liar.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel on seeing the bedsheet?
qa.a: Sarita might feel relieved and a bit embarrassed that the white shape was only a sheet.

grounding: Shows a teenager recalling a vivid event she only heard others describe, blended through group retelling.

passage:
Friday night

Weirdest thing today. At lunch, Dilnaz and the others were talking about the school trip to the fort last month. They said the guide slipped on the stairs and his cap flew off and landed on Rafi's head. Everybody was laughing.

I laughed too, and I could totally see it. The cap, Rafi's face.

Then on the bus I remembered. I was at the back with a headache. I didn't go up those stairs at all. I was in the bus with the teacher.

But I can SEE it. How do I have a memory of something I wasn't at?

I think hearing it so many times made it my memory too. Kind of scary. — Jeevan

qa.q: Where did the guide's cap land?
qa.a: It landed on Rafi's head.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel after remembering the headache on the bus?
qa.a: Jeevan felt puzzled and a bit scared, because the story felt like a real memory even though Jeevan wasn't there.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do when retelling group stories in future?
qa.a: Jeevan could check which parts were actually seen and which were only heard from friends.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel on hearing about the mix-up?
qa.a: Dilnaz might be surprised and find it funny, or realise Dilnaz's own memory could be mixed too.

grounding: A teenager hearing friends retell a trip starts to remember a scene only they described.

passage:
In their small town, the cricket match against the next village had become a legend. Mohit's friends told it at every tea stall: the dog that ran onto the pitch, the six that broke a bicycle bell, the umpire falling off his chair.

Mohit loved the story. By the third week, he was telling it too, adding the dog's name and the colour of the bell.

Then his cousin Tanuja, who had filmed some of it, showed him the video. No dog. The bell was fine. The umpire only wobbled.

"But I remember the dog!" Mohit said.

"You were there, Mohit. But the dog came from Suresh's version."

Mohit watched the video twice, feeling oddly cheated by his own head.

qa.q: What did Tanuja's video show about the bell?
qa.a: The bell was fine.

qa.q: Why did Mohit feel cheated by his own head?
qa.a: He felt shocked and a bit let down, because the story he had heard from friends had mixed into what he truly remembered.

qa.q: What could Mohit do next time the group retells a big event?
qa.a: He could enjoy the story but check photos or videos before adding details as fact.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel showing Mohit the video?
qa.a: Tanuja might feel amused, and maybe a little sorry to spoil the legend.

grounding: A teenager hears friends retell a match and starts remembering details only they described.

passage: The Year 10 camping trip had been two weeks earlier, but at every lunch in the Melbourne school canteen the story grew. "The possum dragged the whole bag of bread up the tree," Tuan said, "and it hissed right at Mr Hale's torch." Everyone laughed. Mateo had been asleep in the tent for most of it. He had only woken to find crumbs outside. Yet when his aunt asked about camp that weekend, Mateo heard himself say, "It hissed right at the torch, this huge grey possum, eyes glowing." He could almost see the eyes. Later, scrolling his own phone photos, he found only one blurry shot of crumbs at dawn. "Wait," he muttered. "Did I actually see any of that?"

qa.q: What did Mateo's own photos show?
qa.a: One blurry shot of crumbs at dawn.

qa.q: How does Mateo feel when he looks at his photos?
qa.a: He feels confused and uneasy, because the possum's glowing eyes felt like his own memory, though he had been asleep in the tent.

qa.q: What could Mateo do when retelling group stories?
qa.a: Separate what he saw from what friends told him, for example, "Tuan says it hissed; I only saw the crumbs."

qa.q: How might Tuan feel if Mateo's version came back to him?
qa.a: Tuan might feel his story had been confirmed by another witness, even though Mateo had only absorbed it from Tuan.

grounding: A teenager starts remembering a possum scene he only heard friends describe, until his photos show otherwise.

passage: At breakfast in the hostel mess, the night's fire drill was already a legend. "The warden came out in a towel and slipped on the stairs," Amandeep said, and the whole table roared. By Wednesday Kunal was telling his roommate the same thing, adding that the towel was blue. Then the counsellor, collecting feedback on the drill, asked Kunal, "What did you see when you came down?" Kunal opened his mouth for the towel story and stopped. He had come down the back staircase. He had not seen the warden at all until the lawn, fully dressed, holding a clipboard. "I think I only heard about the towel," he said, cheeks burning.

qa.q: Which staircase did Kunal come down?
qa.a: The back staircase.

qa.q: Why did Kunal's cheeks burn?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed on realising that the towel story he had told as his own came from Amandeep; he had only seen the warden fully dressed on the lawn.

qa.q: What small habit could help Kunal?
qa.a: Before retelling, ask "did I see this or hear it?" and say "Amandeep says..." when a detail is someone else's.

qa.q: How might the warden feel about the story going round?
qa.a: The warden might feel embarrassed or disrespected by a funny tale that is not even true.

grounding: A teenager retells a friend's version of a fire drill, even adding a detail, as his own memory until an open question stops him.

passage:
Dear Rekha,
Something strange happened, and you're the only one I can ask. You remember when our school bus broke down near the ghats in Class 9? For two years I've told everyone that a monkey snatched the monitor's tiffin and we all chased it. I could describe its face. Yesterday the monitor laughed and said, "That was the others' story, Parveen. You were asleep on the back seat." I felt dizzy. I've heard the story so many times in our group that it moved into my own head as if I'd lived it. So, honestly: were you awake? What do you actually remember? I don't want to keep telling it wrong.
Your friend,
Parveen

qa.q: Where did the school bus break down?
qa.a: Near the ghats, in Class 9.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel on hearing it was the group's story?
qa.a: Parveen felt dizzy and unsettled, because the monkey's face felt personally remembered even though it came from the group's retelling.

qa.q: What is Parveen doing that helps?
qa.a: Asking Rekha what Rekha actually remembers, and choosing not to keep telling it wrong, checks the memory against another witness.

qa.q: How might the monitor see Parveen's version?
qa.a: The monitor finds it funny rather than dishonest, knowing Parveen was asleep and simply soaked up the group's story.

grounding: A teenager realises that a vivid monkey story came from friends' retellings, not from personal memory.

passage:
"So, Madhav, you want to know why I fought with my own cousin? Okay. Remember our Eid trip to the lake, when the boat drifted off? Afterwards Rizwan and Faiz told it at every family dinner: the oar floating away, the swan that hissed, Faiz standing up and nearly falling in.
Yesterday I was telling it to Ammi's friends, and I described the swan hissing at me, its orange beak, everything. Then my cousin Sana said, 'Tanvir, you were asleep in the tent. You only came out when they were back on shore.'
I got so angry. I could see that swan! But she showed me the photos, and there I am in my sleeping bag in the background of one, with the boat far out on the water.
Now I honestly don't know which parts are mine and which are theirs."

qa.q: Where does the photo show Tanvir?
qa.a: In a sleeping bag in the background of one photo, with the boat far out on the water.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir get so angry at Sana?
qa.a: The swan felt like Tanvir's own vivid memory, so being told it came from other people's stories felt insulting and unsettling.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do when telling shared stories in future?
qa.a: Tanvir could mark the parts heard from Rizwan and Faiz, and check photos or ask the people who were actually there.

qa.q: How might Sana have felt when Tanvir got angry?
qa.a: Sana may have felt awkward or defensive, which is why she showed the photos.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after hearing others retell a shared trip many times, remembers scenes only they described.
